items.stem: Explain why this conclusion is weak and how it could be improved: ‘To conclude, I have said that cars are bad, pollution is bad and parking is bad.’
items.answer: Weakness: repetitive list of points; no development or memorable close. Model: A city centre should be a place to meet, not a place to queue. Removing cars is not an attack on drivers; it is an invitation to everyone else.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: identifies the weakness; specific improvement; credit for linking to impact on the reader.

items.stem: Read ‘the lake is a sheet of pewter’ from a descriptive piece, ‘The Frozen Lake at Dawn’. Name the language feature, quote the key words and explain how they shape the reader’s response.
items.answer: Metaphor (‘a sheet of pewter’): the dull, grey metal suggests a cold, hard, motionless surface.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for naming the technique (metaphor); 1 for selecting the key words ‘a sheet of pewter’; remaining mark(s) for analysis of the effect, e.g. the dull, grey metal suggests a cold, hard, motionless surface.

items.stem: ‘Then, very softly, the floor began to tilt.’ (a narrative extract, ‘Floor Nineteen’). What does the phrase ‘the floor began to tilt’ suggest, and how might it make the reader feel?
items.answer: ending on a quiet but terrifying movement leaves the reader in suspense.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for an accurate meaning or connotation of ‘the floor began to tilt’; 1 for the effect on the reader, mood or idea created. Model point: ending on a quiet but terrifying movement leaves the reader in suspense. Credit any valid interpretation supported by the words.

items.stem: What is the usual effect of a sequence of short sentences in a tense moment?
options: It makes the writing more formal
It speeds up the pace and creates tension
It slows the pace and relaxes the reader
items.answer: It speeds up the pace and creates tension
items.markingKey: Short sentences fragment the action and increase urgency.

items.stem: Which feature is most typical of a speech rather than an article?
options: Direct address to a listening audience with signposting
items.answer: Direct address to a listening audience with signposting
items.markingKey: Speeches are written to be heard.

items.stem: ‘Tourism does more harm than good.’ Write an argumentative essay in which you persuade the reader to agree with you. Use a range of evidence and rhetorical devices. Write about 250–350 words.
items.answer: Model approach: rhetorical hook; clear thesis; each paragraph a point + evidence + explanation; devices such as antithesis and tricolon used sparingly; rebuttal; memorable final line.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10: Content and structure 4 marks, Style and accuracy 6 marks. Content and structure (W1–W2) – top band (3–4): a clear, sustained point of view; well-developed reasons supported by evidence; counter-arguments anticipated and rebutted; logical, cohesive paragraphs and a strong conclusion; middle band (2): a clear view with some supporting reasons and evidence; some development; paragraphs mostly logical; lower band (1): a simple view with few or undeveloped reasons; limited organisation. Style and accuracy – top band (5–6): vocabulary is wide, precise and used for deliberate effect; sentence structures are varied and controlled to create effects; register is consistently appropriate; spelling, punctuation and grammar are almost always accurate (W3–W5); middle band (3–4): vocabulary is generally appropriate with some ambition; some variety of sentence structure; register mostly appropriate; errors are occasional and minor (W3–W5); lower band (1–2): vocabulary is simple or imprecise; sentence structures are repetitive; register may be inconsistent; frequent errors sometimes affect clarity (W3–W5). Indicative content: clear, consistent stance; developed reasons with evidence and examples; rhetorical devices used with control; counter-arguments anticipated and rebutted; cohesive paragraphing; persuasive conclusion.

items.stem: Analyse how the writer uses language in these two quotations from a descriptive piece, ‘Ward Seven, 3 a.m.’: (i) ‘a slow scrape like a spade in gravel’ (ii) ‘the hospital corridor is a long, white throat, swallowing sound’ Identify a technique in each and explain its effect.
items.answer: (i) Simile: the harsh, effortful sound conveys illness and quietly suggests digging, an image linked to death. (ii) Metaphor: the corridor seems to devour noise and the narrator, creating a sinister, sterile silence.
items.markingKey: Award up to 10 marks from: for each quotation, 1 for the technique (simile; metaphor) and 1 for an explanation of its effect; remaining mark(s) for a developed point linking both to the mood or purpose of the text.

items.stem: A boy has secretly trained for months to enter a running race his parents forbade. Write the final section of this story (a circular ending), making sure the ending has impact. Write about 250–350 words.
items.answer: Model approach: bring the central conflict to a head; choose a a circular ending; end with an image or line that echoes the opening or theme.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10: Content and structure 4 marks, Style and accuracy 6 marks. Content and structure (W1–W2) – top band (3–4): an engaging, well-developed story with a clear, controlled structure; convincing characters and setting; tension or interest sustained; an effective ending; middle band (2): a clear story with some development of character and setting; structure mostly secure but pace may be uneven; lower band (1): a simple sequence of events with little development; structure unclear or ending abrupt. Style and accuracy – top band (5–6): vocabulary is wide, precise and used for deliberate effect; sentence structures are varied and controlled to create effects; register is consistently appropriate; spelling, punctuation and grammar are almost always accurate (W3–W5); middle band (3–4): vocabulary is generally appropriate with some ambition; some variety of sentence structure; register mostly appropriate; errors are occasional and minor (W3–W5); lower band (1–2): vocabulary is simple or imprecise; sentence structures are repetitive; register may be inconsistent; frequent errors sometimes affect clarity (W3–W5). Indicative content: engaging opening; convincing characters and setting; deliberate structure with a clear turning point; controlled pace and tension; effective, earned ending; narrative voice sustained. Ending type: a circular ending; earned by earlier events.

items.stem: Improve this extract so that it meets W5 (make accurate use of spelling, punctuation and grammar) more successfully, then explain one change you made: ‘Its been a long time since there was rain, the crops are dying and the farmers is worried.’
items.answer: Model: It has been a long time since it rained; the crops are dying and the farmers are worried. The weakness was that there are errors of apostrophe (Its), a comma splice and subject–verb agreement (farmers is).
items.markingKey: Award up to 10 marks from: a rewrite that clearly addresses W5; meaning kept or developed; explanation of the improvement; no new errors.

items.stem: In a narrative extract, ‘My Brother the Genius’ the writer uses the irony ‘only because the watch is cheap’: ‘It did not, he says, but only because the watch is cheap.’ Explain what it suggests to the reader.
items.answer: the narrator reports Femi’s excuse with mock seriousness, highlighting his absurd logic.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: 1 for an accurate meaning or connotation of ‘only because the watch is cheap’. Model point: the narrator reports Femi’s excuse with mock seriousness, highlighting his absurd logic. Credit any valid interpretation supported by the words.

items.stem: Rewrite this passage, varying the sentence structures to create a more powerful effect. ‘The market opens at six. People arrive. They set up stalls. It gets noisy.’
items.answer: Model: At six, as the first grey light seeps over the rooftops, the traders arrive; within minutes tarpaulins snap open, crates thud onto trestles and the square erupts into a hundred bargaining voices.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: Award for a deliberate range of structures (e.g. fronted clauses, periodic sentence, minor sentence) that clearly enhances effect; accurate punctuation. Accept any version that meets the instruction and keeps the meaning; deduct for new errors.

items.stem: In an article by a planetary scientist, ‘Why We Must Keep Looking Up’, the writer states: ‘Abandoning space would save little and cost us our future.’ Explain why a reader might question this claim.
items.answer: An exaggerated conclusion presented as fact.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: identifies the weakness (generalisation, lack of evidence, exaggeration, false choice); explains why it reduces the claim’s reliability; may suggest what evidence is needed.

items.stem: Which phrase best introduces a concession before a rebuttal?
items.answer: Admittedly,
items.markingKey: Concede, then rebut: ‘Admittedly… however…’.

items.stem: Which is usually more effective in a description?
items.answer: One precise, original image
items.markingKey: Precision and control score higher than quantity (W3).

items.stem: Write a story with the title ‘Breaking Point’. Write about 250–350 words.
items.answer: Model approach for ‘Breaking Point’: plan a single focused conflict; hook in the first line; build to a clear climax; resolve with an image or line that links back to the title.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10: Content and structure 4 marks, Style and accuracy 6 marks. Content and structure (W1–W2) – top band (3–4): an engaging, well-developed story with a clear, controlled structure; convincing characters and setting; tension or interest sustained; an effective ending; middle band (2): a clear story with some development of character and setting; structure mostly secure but pace may be uneven; lower band (1): a simple sequence of events with little development; structure unclear or ending abrupt. Style and accuracy – top band (5–6): vocabulary is wide, precise and used for deliberate effect; sentence structures are varied and controlled to create effects; register is consistently appropriate; spelling, punctuation and grammar are almost always accurate (W3–W5); middle band (3–4): vocabulary is generally appropriate with some ambition; some variety of sentence structure; register mostly appropriate; errors are occasional and minor (W3–W5); lower band (1–2): vocabulary is simple or imprecise; sentence structures are repetitive; register may be inconsistent; frequent errors sometimes affect clarity (W3–W5). Indicative content: engaging opening; convincing characters and setting; deliberate structure with a clear turning point; controlled pace and tension; effective, earned ending; narrative voice sustained.

items.stem: Rewrite this sentence so that its register suits a report to the school board, and explain two choices you made: ‘Loads of kids reckon the canteen food is pretty rubbish these days.’
items.answer: Model: A significant proportion of students surveyed expressed dissatisfaction with the current canteen menu.
items.markingKey: Award up to 10 marks from: register appropriate to a report to the school board; meaning kept; two explained choices (vocabulary, contractions, sentence length, address).

items.stem: Text A: ‘Space exploration is not a luxury; it is an investment. Satellites developed for space now forecast storms, guide farmers and connect remote villages to the internet. Research for space missions has helped improve water-purification methods and medical imaging. Studying other planets helps us understand climate change on our own. And exploration inspires: countless young people choose to study science because of a rocket launch or a photograph of Earth from space. The cost sounds enormous, but space agencies usually receive well under one per cent of national budgets. Abandoning space would save little and cost us our future.’ Text B: ‘While billions are spent sending robots to Mars, millions of people on Earth lack clean water. That is not a choice I can defend. Supporters of space programmes point to useful inventions, but many of those could have been developed more cheaply by funding the research directly. Private companies are now racing to launch rockets, so governments need not compete with them. If we want to inspire young people, let them see us solve the climate crisis, end hunger and rebuild crumbling schools. Mars will still be there in fifty years; the communities flooded by rising seas may not be.’ You are a resident who has followed the debate closely. Write a speech for a youth parliament debate on whether governments should spend money on space exploration, evaluating both texts. Pay particular attention to the conventions of a speech and to a voice and register suited to members of a youth parliament. In your speech you should: explain which ideas you agree with and why; consider who would be most affected by the decision; identify and challenge any weak or one-sided evidence. Base your answer on what you have read in both texts, but use your own words. Write about 250–350 words.
items.answer: Model approach: open in role (speech to members of a youth parliament); summarise the issue; evaluate Text A’s strongest points and weaknesses, then Text B’s; weigh them and give a clear, reasoned judgement of your own; close with a recommendation. Conventions: greeting to the audience, direct address, rhetorical devices, signposting for listeners, memorable ending with thanks or a call to action.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10: Reading 4 marks, Writing 6 marks. Reading – top band (3–4): ideas from both texts selected, developed and critically evaluated; a clear, sustained judgement of your own; middle band (2): relevant ideas from both texts with some evaluation; lower band (1): ideas mostly repeated from the texts with little evaluation. Writing – top band (5–6): form, voice and register consistently suited to the audience and purpose; well structured and cohesive; precise, varied language; accurate; middle band (3–4): mostly appropriate form and register; clear structure; generally accurate; lower band (1–2): form or register insecure; loosely organised; errors affect clarity. Indicative reading content: Text A – satellites for weather, farming, internet; spin-offs (water purification, medical imaging); helps understand climate change; inspires young scientists; small share of national budgets. Text B – money could provide clean water; inventions could be funded directly; private companies can take over; inspiration from solving Earth’s problems; urgency of climate crisis. Evaluation – ‘countless’ is vague and the link is not evidenced; an exaggerated conclusion presented as fact; a hypothetical claim with no evidence; presents a false choice: space spending versus clean water. Writing: greeting to the audience, direct address, rhetorical devices, signposting for listeners, memorable ending with thanks or a call to action; register suited to members of a youth parliament.

items.stem: Develop this undeveloped claim into a persuasive point with a reason, evidence or example and an explanation. ‘Fast fashion harms the planet.’
items.answer: Model: Cheap clothing encourages people to buy and discard garments quickly; the textile industry uses vast amounts of water and many items end up in landfill within a year.
items.markingKey: Award up to 10 marks from: Award for a clear reason, specific evidence or example, explanation of why it matters, and controlled persuasive language. Accept any version that meets the instruction and keeps the meaning; deduct for new errors.

items.stem: Identify and explain the error in this sentence, then correct it: ‘Walking into the room, the smell of smoke was overwhelming.’
items.answer: Error: dangling modifier: the smell was not walking. Corrected: ‘Walking into the room, I noticed that the smell of smoke was overwhelming.’
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: names the error; explains the rule; gives a correct version.

items.stem: Identify the structure in this plan and explain one advantage and one risk of using it in an exam composition: ‘An old woman tells her granddaughter the story of her journey across the border; we return to them at the end.’
items.answer: Frame narrative: a story within a story, framed by the present-day conversation. Risk: confusing time shifts or running out of words before the resolution.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for frame narrative; 1 for an advantage; 1 for a risk; further marks for developed explanation.

items.stem: This sentence is narrative: ‘The night before the deadline, Leila stared at her unfinished homework and felt the panic rise.’ Explain how its stance and tone show this.
items.answer: Narrative: tells a story about a character.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for identifying narrative; further mark(s) for explaining the effect or clue: tells a story about a character.

items.stem: Which sentence shows evaluation rather than summary?
options: Text A says students read more.
Text A’s claim that every student reads more is weakened by the lack of any evidence beyond one class.
items.answer: Text A’s claim that every student reads more is weakened by the lack of any evidence beyond one class.
items.markingKey: It judges the quality of evidence.

items.stem: What does a ‘sense of place’ mean in descriptive writing?
options: the reader can vividly imagine a specific, believable location
the place is described in one sentence
the writer names a famous city
items.answer: the reader can vividly imagine a specific, believable location
items.markingKey: Specific, concrete details create it.

items.stem: Write a descriptive piece about a hospital waiting room at night, using a deliberate variety of sentence structures (including at least one periodic sentence and one minor sentence) to control pace and atmosphere. Write about 250–350 words.
items.answer: Model approach: open with a long, cumulative sentence that establishes a hospital waiting room at night; shift to short sentences at the key moment; end with a minor sentence or a periodic sentence for impact.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10: Content and structure 4 marks, Style and accuracy 6 marks. Content and structure (W1–W2) – top band (3–4): a vivid, coherent picture built through carefully selected sensory detail and imagery; strong atmosphere; deliberate shifts of focus give structure; middle band (2): a clear description with some effective detail and imagery; some atmosphere; may drift into narrative; lower band (1): a list-like description with limited detail and little atmosphere; may turn into a story. Style and accuracy – top band (5–6): vocabulary is wide, precise and used for deliberate effect; sentence structures are varied and controlled to create effects; register is consistently appropriate; spelling, punctuation and grammar are almost always accurate (W3–W5); middle band (3–4): vocabulary is generally appropriate with some ambition; some variety of sentence structure; register mostly appropriate; errors are occasional and minor (W3–W5); lower band (1–2): vocabulary is simple or imprecise; sentence structures are repetitive; register may be inconsistent; frequent errors sometimes affect clarity (W3–W5). Indicative content: sentence structures varied purposefully; pace controlled; atmosphere sustained; no slide into narrative.

items.stem: Identify the narrative voice, explain how it is created, and rewrite the extract using a different voice: ‘Mummy says Uncle Joe has gone to live on a farm far away, which is strange because he hated cows.’
items.answer: Naive narrator: the child does not understand what the reader can infer (Uncle Joe has probably died). The rewrite should change perspective, vocabulary and attitude consistently.
items.markingKey: Award up to 10 marks from: 1 for naive narrator; 1 for how it is created; remaining mark(s) for a consistent rewrite in a new voice.

items.stem: Write a discursive essay on part-time jobs for teenagers, considering arguments for and against before reaching a conclusion. Write about 250–350 words.
items.answer: Model approach: introduction framing the debate on part-time jobs for teenagers; paragraph(s) for (skills, money, independence); paragraph(s) against (tiredness, grades, exploitation); evaluation; reasoned conclusion.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10: Content and structure 4 marks, Style and accuracy 6 marks. Content and structure (W1–W2) – top band (3–4): both sides explored fairly and in depth with evidence; points weighed against each other; a reasoned judgement reached in the conclusion; cohesive paragraphing; middle band (2): both sides covered with some development; structure clear though weighing of points is limited; lower band (1): mainly one side or a list of points; little development or evaluation. Style and accuracy – top band (5–6): vocabulary is wide, precise and used for deliberate effect; sentence structures are varied and controlled to create effects; register is consistently appropriate; spelling, punctuation and grammar are almost always accurate (W3–W5); middle band (3–4): vocabulary is generally appropriate with some ambition; some variety of sentence structure; register mostly appropriate; errors are occasional and minor (W3–W5); lower band (1–2): vocabulary is simple or imprecise; sentence structures are repetitive; register may be inconsistent; frequent errors sometimes affect clarity (W3–W5). Indicative content: balanced exploration of both sides with evidence; points weighed and evaluated; measured, objective tone; discourse markers for structure; reasoned judgement in the conclusion. For: skills, money, independence. Against: tiredness, grades, exploitation.

items.stem: Identify the form of this opening, explain its features and rewrite it as the opening of a different form (letter, speech, article or report): ‘This report summarises the findings of a survey of 200 students about the proposed closure of the youth centre and makes three recommendations.’
items.answer: Report: impersonal, formal register; clear statement of scope and purpose. The rewrite should adopt the conventions of the new form.
items.markingKey: Award up to 10 marks from: 1 for the form (report); 1 for features; remaining mark(s) for a convincing rewrite in a new form.

items.stem: Explain why this conclusion is weak and how it could be improved: ‘In conclusion, also another reason is that zoos are expensive.’
items.answer: Weakness: introduces a new point instead of concluding. Model: Zoos can still play a role, but only as sanctuaries for species that truly need them – anything more is entertainment dressed as conservation.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: identifies the weakness; specific improvement; credit for linking to impact on the reader.

items.stem: You are writing a speech to students at a school assembly about teenagers having part-time jobs. Write one paragraph that refers to this claim from Text A, ‘Most students can easily manage eight hours a week without their studies suffering’, and evaluates it in your own words.
items.answer: Model: the paragraph acknowledges the claim, then evaluates it (a generalisation that ignores differences in workload and circumstances), and links to the writer’s own view in an appropriate speech register.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: claim conveyed in own words; evaluation (a generalisation that ignores differences in workload and circumstances); register suited to students at a school assembly; link to the overall argument.

items.stem: ‘The horizon bruises purple.’ (a descriptive piece, ‘The First Rain’). What does the phrase ‘bruises’ suggest, and how might it make the reader feel?
items.answer: the sky seems injured and swollen, hinting at the violence of the coming storm.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for an accurate meaning or connotation of ‘bruises’; 1 for the effect on the reader, mood or idea created. Model point: the sky seems injured and swollen, hinting at the violence of the coming storm. Credit any valid interpretation supported by the words.

items.stem: What does an open ending do?
options: tells the reader exactly what happens to every character
leaves some questions deliberately unanswered for the reader
items.answer: leaves some questions deliberately unanswered for the reader
items.markingKey: Effective when it feels intentional, not unfinished.

items.stem: Which sentence uses the apostrophe correctly?
options: The children’s’ coats were hung by the door.
The childrens coats were hung by the door.
The childrens’ coats were hung by the door.
The children’s coats were hung by the door.
items.answer: The children’s coats were hung by the door.
items.markingKey: Irregular plural + ’s.

items.stem: Write a discursive essay on banning mobile phones in schools, considering arguments for and against before reaching a conclusion. Write about 250–350 words.
items.answer: Model approach: introduction framing the debate on banning mobile phones in schools; paragraph(s) for (concentration, less cyberbullying); paragraph(s) against (safety, learning tools, independence); evaluation; reasoned conclusion.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10: Content and structure 4 marks, Style and accuracy 6 marks. Content and structure (W1–W2) – top band (3–4): both sides explored fairly and in depth with evidence; points weighed against each other; a reasoned judgement reached in the conclusion; cohesive paragraphing; middle band (2): both sides covered with some development; structure clear though weighing of points is limited; lower band (1): mainly one side or a list of points; little development or evaluation. Style and accuracy – top band (5–6): vocabulary is wide, precise and used for deliberate effect; sentence structures are varied and controlled to create effects; register is consistently appropriate; spelling, punctuation and grammar are almost always accurate (W3–W5); middle band (3–4): vocabulary is generally appropriate with some ambition; some variety of sentence structure; register mostly appropriate; errors are occasional and minor (W3–W5); lower band (1–2): vocabulary is simple or imprecise; sentence structures are repetitive; register may be inconsistent; frequent errors sometimes affect clarity (W3–W5). Indicative content: balanced exploration of both sides with evidence; points weighed and evaluated; measured, objective tone; discourse markers for structure; reasoned judgement in the conclusion. For: concentration, less cyberbullying. Against: safety, learning tools, independence.

items.stem: Text A on replacing school textbooks with tablets argues: ‘interactive diagrams and videos’. Text B argues: ‘distraction from notifications’. Text A: ‘Last year my class swapped printed textbooks for tablets, and I will never go back. A single tablet holds every book a student needs, so no more aching backs from overloaded bags. Digital texts are updated instantly, while our old geography books still described a country that changed its name a decade ago. Interactive diagrams and videos bring difficult ideas to life, and students who struggle can listen to texts read aloud. Of course, screens can distract, but that is a matter of teaching discipline, not a reason to stay in the past. Every student in my class now reads more. The future of learning is digital; schools that refuse to accept this are failing their students.’ Text B: ‘Before schools rush to replace books with tablets, they should look at the evidence. Several studies suggest that students remember more of what they read on paper than on screen, particularly for long, complex texts. Tablets are expensive to buy, insure and repair, and a broken screen can leave a student without any books at all. Many families cannot afford reliable internet at home, so “digital homework” widens the gap between rich and poor. Teachers also report that notifications and games compete constantly for attention. This is not an argument against technology, which has real value for research and accessibility. It is an argument for balance: keep printed books at the heart of learning and use tablets where they genuinely help.’ Which point do you find more convincing, and why? Refer to the evidence in both texts.
items.answer: Either view may be argued if supported: weigh the evidence offered for each (Text A is strongly in favour of tablets; Text B is cautious and largely against). Weaknesses: an unsupported generalisation based on one class, with no evidence of how reading was measured; an exaggerated claim that presents a false choice between tablets and failure; dismisses a serious concern (distraction) without evidence; the studies are not named or quantified, so the reader cannot judge them; anecdotal reports; ‘constantly’ may exaggerate
items.markingKey: Award up to 10 marks from: clear judgement; evidence from both texts; evaluation of the quality of evidence; recognition of bias or perspective.

items.stem: Describe a beach at the end of the holiday season. Focus on creating a strong atmosphere and a vivid sense of place. Write about 250–350 words.
items.answer: Model approach: choose one dominant atmosphere; open with a striking image; build detail through the senses; vary sentence length to control mood; end on an image that crystallises the atmosphere.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10: Content and structure 4 marks, Style and accuracy 6 marks. Content and structure (W1–W2) – top band (3–4): a vivid, coherent picture built through carefully selected sensory detail and imagery; strong atmosphere; deliberate shifts of focus give structure; middle band (2): a clear description with some effective detail and imagery; some atmosphere; may drift into narrative; lower band (1): a list-like description with limited detail and little atmosphere; may turn into a story. Style and accuracy – top band (5–6): vocabulary is wide, precise and used for deliberate effect; sentence structures are varied and controlled to create effects; register is consistently appropriate; spelling, punctuation and grammar are almost always accurate (W3–W5); middle band (3–4): vocabulary is generally appropriate with some ambition; some variety of sentence structure; register mostly appropriate; errors are occasional and minor (W3–W5); lower band (1–2): vocabulary is simple or imprecise; sentence structures are repetitive; register may be inconsistent; frequent errors sometimes affect clarity (W3–W5). Indicative content: focus on a specific place and moment; carefully selected sensory detail; original imagery; deliberate structure (shifts of time, focus or scale); atmosphere sustained; does not become a story.

items.stem: Analyse how the writer uses language in these two quotations from a narrative extract, ‘Auntie Grace Arrives’: (i) ‘“Tired?” said Auntie Grace, handing me a suitcase’ (ii) ‘handing me a suitcase that weighed as much as I did’ Identify a technique in each and explain its effect.
items.answer: (i) Dialogue: echoing the mother’s word as a question shows Grace’s sharp, combative wit. (ii) Hyperbole: the exaggeration adds humour and shows Grace treating the narrator as a porter.
items.markingKey: Award up to 10 marks from: for each quotation, 1 for the technique (dialogue; hyperbole) and 1 for an explanation of its effect; remaining mark(s) for a developed point linking both to the mood or purpose of the text.

items.stem: A student ends an argumentative essay with this sentence: ‘In conclusion, there are good and bad points.’ Explain what makes it an ineffective conclusion.
items.answer: Vague; no judgement or weighing.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: identifies the weakness (vague; no judgement or weighing); explains its effect on the reader’s final impression.

items.stem: Identify the technique, analyse its effect, and continue the extract for two or three sentences, maintaining the tension: ‘The boat would leave at six. It was ten to, and we were still two kilometres away.’
items.answer: A ticking clock: a deadline creates urgency. Continuation should sustain the technique.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for a ticking clock; 1 for effect; remaining mark(s) for a continuation that sustains tension.

items.stem: In a letter to a newspaper from a long-time island resident, the writer states: ‘A second cruise terminal would turn our home into a theme park.’ Explain why a reader might question this claim.
items.answer: Emotive hyperbole rather than evidence.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: identifies the weakness (generalisation, lack of evidence, exaggeration, false choice); explains why it reduces the claim’s reliability; may suggest what evidence is needed.

items.stem: Which tense is often effective for descriptive writing because it creates immediacy?
items.answer: The present tense
items.markingKey: E.g. ‘The market wakes…’.

items.stem: Which of these best describes ‘deliberate effect’ in W2?
options: Choices of structure made on purpose to influence the reader
Copying the structure of the source text
items.answer: Choices of structure made on purpose to influence the reader
items.markingKey: E.g. delaying a revelation, a one-line paragraph, a circular ending.

items.stem: Write a story in which most of the tension comes from a conversation between a student and a teacher who suspects them of cheating. Write about 250–350 words.
items.answer: Model approach: establish setting briefly; let the conversation between a student and a teacher who suspects them of cheating carry the conflict; use subtext, interruptions and silences; end on a line of dialogue or a telling action.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10: Content and structure 4 marks, Style and accuracy 6 marks. Content and structure (W1–W2) – top band (3–4): an engaging, well-developed story with a clear, controlled structure; convincing characters and setting; tension or interest sustained; an effective ending; middle band (2): a clear story with some development of character and setting; structure mostly secure but pace may be uneven; lower band (1): a simple sequence of events with little development; structure unclear or ending abrupt. Style and accuracy – top band (5–6): vocabulary is wide, precise and used for deliberate effect; sentence structures are varied and controlled to create effects; register is consistently appropriate; spelling, punctuation and grammar are almost always accurate (W3–W5); middle band (3–4): vocabulary is generally appropriate with some ambition; some variety of sentence structure; register mostly appropriate; errors are occasional and minor (W3–W5); lower band (1–2): vocabulary is simple or imprecise; sentence structures are repetitive; register may be inconsistent; frequent errors sometimes affect clarity (W3–W5). Indicative content: engaging opening; convincing characters and setting; deliberate structure with a clear turning point; controlled pace and tension; effective, earned ending; narrative voice sustained. Dialogue punctuated accurately; each voice distinct; subtext and gesture used.

items.stem: These paragraph topics for an argumentative essay on banning cars from city centres are jumbled. A: conclusion and call to action B: introduction and stance C: strongest reason: air quality, with evidence D: second reason: safety and space E: counter-argument (businesses) and rebuttal Put them in the most effective order and explain the structural principle you used.
items.answer: BCDEA – logical argument with rebuttal before the conclusion.
items.markingKey: Award up to 10 marks from: correct or justifiable order (BCDEA); explanation of the structural principle (logical argument with rebuttal before the conclusion); comment on the effect of the opening and ending.

items.stem: ‘Space exploration is a waste of money.’ Write a discursive essay exploring different views on this statement. Write about 250–350 words.
items.answer: Model approach: introduce the debate; arguments for with evidence; arguments against with evidence; weigh the strongest points; reasoned conclusion.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10: Content and structure 4 marks, Style and accuracy 6 marks. Content and structure (W1–W2) – top band (3–4): both sides explored fairly and in depth with evidence; points weighed against each other; a reasoned judgement reached in the conclusion; cohesive paragraphing; middle band (2): both sides covered with some development; structure clear though weighing of points is limited; lower band (1): mainly one side or a list of points; little development or evaluation. Style and accuracy – top band (5–6): vocabulary is wide, precise and used for deliberate effect; sentence structures are varied and controlled to create effects; register is consistently appropriate; spelling, punctuation and grammar are almost always accurate (W3–W5); middle band (3–4): vocabulary is generally appropriate with some ambition; some variety of sentence structure; register mostly appropriate; errors are occasional and minor (W3–W5); lower band (1–2): vocabulary is simple or imprecise; sentence structures are repetitive; register may be inconsistent; frequent errors sometimes affect clarity (W3–W5). Indicative content: balanced exploration of both sides with evidence; points weighed and evaluated; measured, objective tone; discourse markers for structure; reasoned judgement in the conclusion.

items.stem: Rewrite this weak ending so that it has more impact. ‘In the end I realised that friendship is the most important thing in the world, and that is the moral of my story.’
items.answer: Model: show the realisation through action, e.g. the narrator walking across to sit with the friend.
items.markingKey: Award up to 10 marks from: Award for an ending that avoids the weakness (states the moral directly; tells rather than shows), is earned by the story and leaves a strong final impression. Accept any version that meets the instruction and keeps the meaning; deduct for new errors.

items.stem: This extract uses focusing on small sensory details: ‘A single bead of sweat ran down the guard’s neck and disappeared into his collar.’ Explain how it builds suspense.
items.answer: Focusing on small sensory details: close focus slows time and heightens tension.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: 1 for identifying focusing on small sensory details; further mark(s) for explaining the effect or clue: close focus slows time and heightens tension.

items.stem: Opponents argue: ‘Zoos are necessary to save endangered species.’ Write a paragraph that concedes any valid part of this argument and then rebuts it convincingly.
items.answer: Model: While some breeding programmes are successful, only a minority of zoo species are part of them; conservation funding could achieve more by protecting habitats directly.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: fair statement of the counter-argument; concession marker; rebuttal with reason or evidence; controlled, persuasive tone.

items.stem: This is a periodic sentence: ‘After the long drive through the rain, after the wrong turnings and the arguments over the map, after the fuel light had glowed for twenty kilometres, we finally saw the lights of the village.’ Explain its effect.
items.answer: Periodic sentence: the main clause is delayed until the end, building anticipation and relief.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for identifying periodic sentence; further mark(s) for explaining the effect or clue: the main clause is delayed until the end, building anticipation and relief.

items.stem: What is the main purpose of dialogue in a short story?
options: To reveal character and move the plot forward
To describe the setting in detail
items.answer: To reveal character and move the plot forward
items.markingKey: Good dialogue does work; avoid small talk.

items.stem: This line comes from a descriptive piece, ‘The Spice Souk’: ‘the noise closes behind you like a door’ Which atmosphere does the piece as a whole create?
items.answer: lively and joyful
items.markingKey: The piece is lively and joyful. Sound closing like a door; light as gold bars; similes of colour; layered smells; touch (paper cone); movement (donkey); breathless final tricolon.

items.stem: Write two short texts on the same subject: (1) a formal email to a museum asking to arrange a class visit; (2) a message to classmates telling them about the visit. Then write a paragraph analysing how and why your vocabulary and register differ. Write about 250–350 words in total.
items.answer: Model approach: text 1 formal (full forms, polite modals, precise nouns, clear purpose and sign-off); text 2 informal and lively (direct address, contractions, colloquial but controlled language); analysis naming specific choices and linking them to audience and purpose.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10: Content and structure 6 marks, Style and accuracy 4 marks. Content and structure – top band (5–6): both texts precisely judged for audience and purpose; analysis perceptive and specific; middle band (3–4): two recognisably different registers; analysis identifies some choices; lower band (1–2): register barely changes; analysis vague. Style and accuracy – top band (3–4): vocabulary is wide, precise and used for deliberate effect; sentence structures are varied and controlled to create effects; register is consistently appropriate; spelling, punctuation and grammar are almost always accurate (W3–W5); middle band (2): vocabulary is generally appropriate with some ambition; some variety of sentence structure; register mostly appropriate; errors are occasional and minor (W3–W5); lower band (1): vocabulary is simple or imprecise; sentence structures are repetitive; register may be inconsistent; frequent errors sometimes affect clarity (W3–W5). Indicative content: formality markers; vocabulary choice; sentence length; modes of address; purpose.

items.stem: You are writing a letter to parents of students about teenagers having part-time jobs. Write one paragraph that refers to this claim from Text A, ‘Employers tell me that applicants with work experience stand out immediately’, and evaluates it in your own words.
items.answer: Model: the paragraph acknowledges the claim, then evaluates it (second-hand, anecdotal evidence), and links to the writer’s own view in an appropriate letter register.
items.markingKey: Award up to 10 marks from: claim conveyed in own words; evaluation (second-hand, anecdotal evidence); register suited to parents of students; link to the overall argument.

items.stem: Write a story with the title ‘The Stranger’. Write about 250–350 words.
items.answer: Model approach for ‘The Stranger’: plan a single focused conflict; hook in the first line; build to a clear climax; resolve with an image or line that links back to the title.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10: Content and structure 4 marks, Style and accuracy 6 marks. Content and structure (W1–W2) – top band (3–4): an engaging, well-developed story with a clear, controlled structure; convincing characters and setting; tension or interest sustained; an effective ending; middle band (2): a clear story with some development of character and setting; structure mostly secure but pace may be uneven; lower band (1): a simple sequence of events with little development; structure unclear or ending abrupt. Style and accuracy – top band (5–6): vocabulary is wide, precise and used for deliberate effect; sentence structures are varied and controlled to create effects; register is consistently appropriate; spelling, punctuation and grammar are almost always accurate (W3–W5); middle band (3–4): vocabulary is generally appropriate with some ambition; some variety of sentence structure; register mostly appropriate; errors are occasional and minor (W3–W5); lower band (1–2): vocabulary is simple or imprecise; sentence structures are repetitive; register may be inconsistent; frequent errors sometimes affect clarity (W3–W5). Indicative content: engaging opening; convincing characters and setting; deliberate structure with a clear turning point; controlled pace and tension; effective, earned ending; narrative voice sustained.

items.stem: Rewrite this one-sided claim as a balanced sentence suitable for a discursive essay. ‘Online learning is far better than classroom teaching.’
items.answer: Model (discursive): Online learning offers flexibility and access to resources, although many students miss the support and social contact of a classroom.
items.markingKey: Award up to 10 marks from: Award for presenting more than one view, measured tone and a discourse marker of contrast. Accept any version that meets the instruction and keeps the meaning; deduct for new errors.
